classes.name: Presidential electors
classes.locator: 3 U.S.C. §§ 1 and 21(1); U.S. Const. art. II, § 1, cl. 2
classes.note: One statewide slate per state (Maine by district from 1972 and Nebraska from 1992 add one per district). Legislatures appointed the electors in some states and years, so those states have no popular vote then.

cadence.locator: 3 U.S.C. § 1 and § 21(1): electors are appointed on election day, the Tuesday next after the first Monday in November every fourth year (uniform day from the Act of January 23, 1845)

appointed.locator: Delaware's legislature chose its electors through 1828 (with South Carolina, the only two states to do so that year)
In 1824 the legislatures of Delaware, Georgia, Louisiana, New York, South Carolina, and Vermont chose the electors; the other eighteen states held a popular vote
South Carolina's legislature chose the state's electors through 1860, the last state to do so
1864: Louisiana's Union legislature named electors without a popular vote, and Congress did not count their votes
1868: Florida's legislature chose the state's electors; no popular vote was held

classes.name: U.S. Senate
classes.locator: U.S. Const. art. I, § 3, cl. 1-2 and amend. XVII
classes.note: Two senators per state in three classes, one class elected every second year for six-year terms; popular election from 1914 under the Seventeenth Amendment.

senate.locator: U.S. Const. art. I, § 3, cl. 2 (senators divided into three classes, one class chosen every second year) and amend. XVII (popular election, ratified April 8, 1913); a state admitted later joins at its first regular election

classes.name: U.S. House of Representatives
classes.locator: U.S. Const. art. I, § 2, cl. 1; 2 U.S.C. § 7
classes.note: Every seat every second year; the seats per state follow each decennial apportionment.

cadence.locator: 2 U.S.C. § 7: the Tuesday next after the first Monday in November in every even numbered year; U.S. Const. art. I, § 2, cl. 1: members chosen every second year

classes.name: Governors
classes.note: Four-year terms everywhere but New Hampshire and Vermont; the year in the four-year cycle differs by state.

governors.locator: Arkansas governors served two-year terms until Amendment 63 (1984), elected in even years through 1984
Arkansas Amendment 63 (1984): four-year terms from the 1986 election
Rhode Island governors served two-year terms through the 1992 election
Rhode Island's 1992 amendment: four-year terms from the 1994 election
Illinois elected governors in presidential years through 1976; the 1970 constitution gave the 1976 winner a two-year term
Illinois Const. 1970 art. V, § 2 and transition schedule: governors elected in midterm years from 1978
American Samoa's first elected governor took office in January 1978; regular four-year elections from 1980

classes.name: Other statewide executive offices
classes.note: Lieutenant governors, attorneys general, secretaries of state, treasurers, auditors, and other offices elected statewide, plus the Council of the District of Columbia.

classes.name: State supreme courts
classes.note: Justices chosen by partisan or nonpartisan election, or retained by retention election; appointed courts hold no elections.

chambers.locator: N.J. Const. art. IV, § II, ¶ 1: senators serve four-year terms, except a two-year first term after each decennial census, so the 2011 apportionment set elections in 2011, 2013, 2017, and 2021
N.J. Const. art. IV, § II, ¶ 1: after the 2021 two-year term, senators elected in 2023 and 2027 serve four-year terms until the post-2030 census term

classes.name: Party offices
classes.note: State and county party committee members and convention delegates chosen on the primary ballot.

classes.name: Town and township offices
classes.note: The archive files towns and townships as municipalities, so their held contests classify as municipal; the class carries the Census roster and its cadence.
